passage:
Note from Urmila, disability support officer, college of engineering, Wednesday.

Hrithik, a first-year, came in with a folder of old school reports and a letter from his doctor about his ADHD. He had clearly rehearsed. He said, 'I'm not asking for less work. I'm asking for a quieter room in exams and permission to break the paper into parts.' His voice shook at the start and steadied as he went on. He said that in school he'd been called lazy and he didn't want to hide it this time. We went through the options the college offers. I explained the process, the forms and who approves them. He asked good questions about deadlines. I have forwarded his request to the exam cell and told him to contact me directly if anything is delayed.

qa.q: What two things did Hrithik ask for?
qa.a: A quieter room in exams and permission to break the paper into parts.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's voice shake at the start?
qa.a: He was nervous, probably because in school he had been called lazy and feared being judged again.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped his request succeed?
qa.a: He came prepared with documents and was clear and specific about what he needed and why.

qa.q: How does Urmila view Hrithik's approach?
qa.a: Urmila sees him as prepared and thoughtful, and responds by explaining the process and staying available to him.

grounding: Shows a student clearly stating his needs to his college and asking for specific exam changes.

passage:
Friday, late

I did it. I told Uday, my manager, about my anxiety. Not the whole story. Just enough.

The open-plan office has been hard. Phones ringing, people laughing, and my chest tight all afternoon. I kept thinking I was bad at the job. My counsellor helped me write down what would actually help: noise-cancelling headphones allowed at my desk, and two days a week from home.

Uday listened. He didn't make a face. He said, 'I wish you'd told me earlier.' He agreed to headphones right away and said he'd check with HR about the home days.

My hands were sweating the whole time. After, I bought myself a samosa to celebrate. Silly, but I felt lighter.

Nilesh, you were braver than you thought.

qa.q: What did Uday agree to straight away?
qa.a: He agreed to let Nilesh use headphones at the desk.

qa.q: What does the celebration samosa show about how Nilesh felt afterward?
qa.a: It shows Nilesh felt relieved and a bit proud, as if something difficult had been achieved.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh prepare for the conversation?
qa.a: Working out with the counsellor exactly what would help, so the request could be specific and practical.

qa.q: How might Uday feel about learning this now?
qa.a: He seems a little sorry Nilesh struggled silently and wants to help, since he said he wished he'd been told earlier.

grounding: Shows a young worker telling his manager about anxiety and asking for specific workplace changes.

passage: At the ITI in Jhunjhunu, the lathe workshop roared all morning, and Sumit caught maybe half of what Urmila madam said. He had worn a hearing aid in one ear since childhood, but in that noise it helped little. For two weeks he copied his neighbour's work and nodded along, stomach tight, afraid of being called slow. Then he misread a measurement and ruined a part. That night, at his uncle's tea stall, he practised the sentence under his breath. The next morning he waited until the others left. 'Madam, I have hearing loss. In the workshop I miss instructions. Could I stand near you, and could you write the measurements on the board?' She looked surprised, then nodded. 'Why didn't you say earlier?' From that week the measurements went up on the board in big chalk. Two other boys used them too.

qa.q: What did Sumit ask Urmila madam for?
qa.a: To stand near her and to have the measurements written on the board.

qa.q: Why did Sumit copy his neighbour and nod along for two weeks?
qa.a: He was anxious about being seen as slow, so he hid that he could not hear the instructions.

qa.q: What helped Sumit ask effectively?
qa.a: Practising the sentence, choosing a private moment, naming his need plainly and suggesting simple, specific adjustments.

qa.q: How did the change affect the other trainees?
qa.a: Two other boys used the board measurements too, showing that an adjustment for one person can help others.

grounding: Shows a trainee with hearing loss overcoming anxiety to ask his institute for simple, reasonable adjustments.

passage: Three weeks into his first job at a logistics office in Toronto, Tariq was drowning in open-plan noise. He had ADHD, known since his school years, and usually managed with lists and quiet. Here phones rang, people chatted at the next desk, and he kept losing track of tasks halfway through. He drafted an email to his manager, Liam, four times, then deleted it, worried he'd look like he wanted special treatment. On Thursday he finally asked for ten minutes. 'I work best with written task lists and less noise. Could I use headphones, and sometimes book the small meeting room for focused work?' Liam listened, asked what else would help, and said, 'That's reasonable. I'd rather know.' He also pointed Tariq to the HR form so it was on record. Tariq walked back to his desk with his hands still shaking, but lighter.

qa.q: What did Tariq ask to use at work?
qa.a: Headphones, and sometimes the small meeting room for focused work.

qa.q: Why did Tariq delete his email four times?
qa.a: He worried he would look like he wanted special treatment, which shows how anxious he felt about asking.

qa.q: What made Tariq's request easy to agree to?
qa.a: He explained how he works best and asked for specific, practical adjustments instead of a vague complaint.

qa.q: How does Liam see Tariq's request?
qa.a: As reasonable and useful to know; he would rather hear it than have Tariq struggle quietly.

grounding: Shows a young employee abroad stating his needs to his manager and asking for reasonable workplace adjustments.

passage: The lecture hall at the engineering college had a ceiling fan that roared and a professor who spoke facing the board. Manoj, who had lost much of the hearing in one ear as a child, caught maybe half of every class. For a month he copied a friend's notes at night and said nothing. Then he missed an announcement about a test and scored a zero. That afternoon he knocked on the door of the student support cell. Himani, the coordinator, listened without hurrying him. "What would help in class?" Manoj had practised this. "A front seat on the left. Slides shared after class. And announcements made facing us." Himani wrote it down. "Those are reasonable. I'll email your department today, and you can bring any problems back here." Manoj walked out with a copy of the email. His hands still shook, but for the first time the zero didn't feel like his fault.

qa.q: What did Manoj score on the test he missed?
qa.a: A zero.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling as he walked out with the email?
qa.a: Manoj felt nervous, hands still shaking, but relieved and less ashamed, no longer blaming himself for the zero.

qa.q: What made Manoj's request easy to act on?
qa.a: He had practised it and asked for specific, reasonable adjustments: a front seat, shared slides, and announcements made facing the class.

qa.q: How does Himani see Manoj's request?
qa.a: Himani treats it as reasonable and part of the support cell's role, listening without hurry and emailing the department that day.

grounding: A student with partial hearing loss states his needs to the college support cell and gets reasonable adjustments.

passage:
Subject: A request about how I work best
Dear Amandeep,
Thank you for my first two weeks. I'm enjoying the team and the work.
I'd like to share something so that I can do my best here. I was diagnosed with ADHD in college. For me, open-plan noise and long unstructured tasks are harder, and I sometimes lose track of spoken instructions. It doesn't affect the quality of what I deliver when things are set up well.
A few adjustments helped me before: headphones or the quiet room for focused work, key tasks in writing after meetings, and big deadlines broken into weekly checkpoints. None of these should cost the team anything.
Honestly, I was nervous about writing this. I'd be grateful for fifteen minutes this week, and I'm happy to involve HR if that's the right process.
Best regards,
Raghav

qa.q: When was Raghav diagnosed?
qa.a: In college.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling while writing the email?
qa.a: Raghav felt nervous about disclosing it, as the email admits, but hopeful enough to ask.

qa.q: What makes Raghav's request effective?
qa.a: It is specific, links each adjustment to how Raghav works best, notes they cost little, and offers a short talk and HR involvement.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel receiving this email?
qa.a: Amandeep would likely appreciate the clarity and honesty, knowing exactly how to help a new team member do well.

grounding: A new employee writes to a manager disclosing ADHD and asking for specific, reasonable adjustments.

passage: Thomas, you know I used to fake being sick every time we had a presentation? That was me, Deepak, three years running. My heart would race, my hands went numb, and once I walked out halfway through a sentence. Last year the college counsellor helped me understand what was happening and work on it. And she said something I'd never considered: "You can ask the department for adjustments." I laughed. Like they'd care. But I wrote to my professor anyway. I asked if I could present to a smaller group first, and keep my notes visible on the screen. She said yes in one line. One line! I'd spent three years hiding. The presentation still made me shake, but I got through it, start to finish. What would I tell anyone? Your need is information, not an excuse. Say it clearly. The worst they can say is no.

qa.q: What did Deepak ask the professor for?
qa.a: To present to a smaller group first and keep notes visible on the screen.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling before presentations in the past?
qa.a: Deepak felt intense fear, with a racing heart and numb hands, enough to fake being sick.

qa.q: What did Deepak learn about asking for adjustments?
qa.a: That a clear, specific request is information, not an excuse, and institutions often agree readily.

qa.q: How might the professor have seen Deepak's request?
qa.a: The professor seems to have found it simple and reasonable, agreeing in one line.

grounding: A student tells a friend how, with a counsellor's help, he asked a professor for adjustments for presentation anxiety.

passage: I sat behind Himani in the exam cell queue, so I heard most of it. She had a thin file with her audiologist's letter on top. When her turn came, she said, "I have moderate hearing loss in both ears. In the hall, I miss announcements, like time warnings and corrections to the paper. Could I sit in the front row, and could the invigilator write changes on the board?" The clerk said something about rules, and Himani didn't raise her voice. She just asked, "Who decides this, so I can send the letter to them?" Her ears went a bit red, and she kept tapping the file. I don't know if she was nervous or just impatient; with Himani, it's hard to tell. The clerk gave her an email address. Outside, she photographed the letter and sent it right there on the steps, then said to me, "Done. Now chai." That's all I saw. I'm Tanuja, and until that day I hadn't noticed how much she misses in our exam hall.

qa.q: What two changes did Himani ask for in the exam hall?
qa.a: She asked to sit in the front row and for the invigilator to write changes on the board.

qa.q: What might Himani have been feeling when her ears went red and she kept tapping the file?
qa.a: She may have felt nervous or uncomfortable having to explain her hearing loss in a queue, or impatient with the rules, but she stayed calm and determined.

qa.q: What did Himani's approach get right when the clerk mentioned rules?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, she asked who decides and sent the letter to that person at once, which kept the request moving.

qa.q: How did watching this change things for Tanuja?
qa.a: Tanuja realised she had never noticed how much Himani misses in the exam hall, so she feels more aware and possibly a little guilty for not seeing it earlier.

grounding: An observer watches a student state her hearing needs to the exam office and ask for reasonable changes calmly and through the right channel.

passage:
Monday. Vishal's first week at the design firm is a blur of sticky notes. Jahnavi, his lead, gives instructions in quick bursts during stand-up; by lunch he has lost half of them and is staying late to rebuild the list from memory. He tells no one about his ADHD.

Thursday of the next week. After another late night, he books ten minutes with Jahnavi. His hands are cold. "I work best when tasks are in writing, and when I'm not right next to the printer," he says. "I have ADHD. I'm not asking for less work, just a clearer way to receive it." Jahnavi nods slowly. "Would a shared task board after stand-up work?" she asks. "And the desk by the window is free."

Three weeks later. The board is up. Vishal leaves at six most days. Two other juniors have started using the board too, and Jahnavi now posts every change there first.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi suggest after Vishal explained what he needed?
qa.a: She suggested a shared task board after stand-up and said the desk by the window is free.

qa.q: Why were Vishal's hands cold when he met Jahnavi?
qa.a: Vishal was anxious about revealing his ADHD at a new job, afraid she might think he wanted less work.

qa.q: What made Vishal's request easy to act on?
qa.a: He named specific changes, written tasks and a quieter desk, and said clearly he was not asking for less work.

qa.q: What is it like for the other juniors once the task board appears?
qa.a: They also benefit from clearer instructions, so the change Vishal asked for ends up helping the whole team, not only him.

grounding: Across three weeks a new employee moves from silent struggle to stating his ADHD needs to his lead and receiving simple workplace adjustments.

passage:
Sit, Vandana, the rice can wait. You asked why your Lokesh Mama never lets anyone call him "poor thing." I'll tell you.

When I was nineteen, my first-year classes were on the third floor, and my leg brace made the stairs take ten minutes each way. I was late every day. One professor marked me absent three times in a row. I was so angry and so ashamed that I nearly left the college.

Then my room-mate said, "They can't fix what they don't know." So I wrote a letter to the principal. I said, plainly, that I could not climb three floors quickly, and asked if our section could use a ground-floor room, or if I could be marked present from the time I reached the stairs.

The principal called me in. He was stiff at first. But the next month our section moved downstairs. Nobody pitied me. They just changed a room.

qa.q: Where were Lokesh's first-year classes held?
qa.a: His first-year classes were on the third floor.

qa.q: How did young Lokesh feel after being marked absent three times?
qa.a: He felt angry and ashamed, so much that he nearly left the college.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Lokesh's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Writing plainly to the principal about the stairs and offering two possible fixes worked because it gave the college clear facts and a practical choice.

qa.q: How might the principal have seen Lokesh's letter at first?
qa.a: The principal was stiff at first, perhaps unused to such a request, but the clear, polite letter made it easy to agree to a simple room change.

grounding: An uncle's memory shows a nineteen-year-old stating a mobility need to a college in writing and asking for a reasonable change.

passage:
Binita had waited months for her first job offer, at an accounts firm. On her first morning, it poured, and the lane outside the office flooded. When she finally got her wheelchair to the building, the lift had a paper sign: Out of order. Her desk was on the second floor.
She sat in the lobby, wet and furious, thinking about going home.
Instead, she called Santosh in HR. She kept her voice steady. "I'm in the lobby. The lift is broken, and I can't get upstairs. I'd like to discuss a ground-floor desk until it's fixed, and a date for the repair."
Santosh came down himself, apologised and set her up in the ground-floor meeting room with a laptop. That afternoon, they wrote down her needs together: a working lift, an accessible washroom key, and a ramp at the side door.
Binita went home tired, but she'd started her job by saying what she needed.

qa.q: What did the paper sign on the lift say?
qa.a: Out of order.

qa.q: How did Binita feel sitting in the lobby?
qa.a: Binita felt furious and discouraged, wet and tempted to go home on her first day.

qa.q: What made Binita's request effective?
qa.a: She calmly stated the problem, asked for a specific adjustment and a repair date, and then wrote down her needs with HR.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt when he saw Binita in the lobby?
qa.a: Santosh was probably embarrassed and apologetic that the firm wasn't ready, and wanted to fix it quickly.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult with a disability stating her needs to an employer and asking for reasonable adjustments despite a hard first day.

passage:
Disha had panic attacks, something she'd known about since school and managed with a counsellor's help. Presentations in front of big groups were the worst trigger.
At her college in Kolkata, the new semester's course required a solo presentation to a hundred students. She spent a week feeling sick about it.
Her counsellor suggested she talk to the professor, not just suffer. So after class she went to Professor Bhavna's office, hands cold. "Ma'am, I have an anxiety condition that makes large presentations very hard. I'm not asking to skip it. Could I present to a smaller group, or record it?"
Professor Bhavna listened, then nodded. "The skill I'm testing is explaining ideas, not surviving a crowd. You can present to ten students in my room."
Disha presented two weeks later. Her voice shook for the first minute. Then it didn't.

qa.q: How many students would the original presentation have been to?
qa.a: A hundred students.

qa.q: How did Disha feel going to Professor Bhavna's office?
qa.a: Disha felt nervous, with cold hands, and afraid of being seen as asking to skip work.

qa.q: Which parts of Disha's request were well made?
qa.a: She named her need clearly, said she wasn't avoiding the task, and offered practical options.

qa.q: How does Professor Bhavna see the adjustment?
qa.a: Professor Bhavna sees it as fair, since the skill being tested is explaining ideas, not coping with a crowd.

grounding: Shows a young adult stating an anxiety-related need to a professor and asking for a reasonable adjustment.

passage:
"Wasim, have you got ten minutes?"
Wasim looked up from his screen. "Sure, Saurabh. What's up?"
"You know I was diagnosed with ADHD last year. I've been managing, but the open office is hard. I lose track of verbal instructions, and the noise makes it harder."
"I didn't realise. What would help?"
"Two things. Could you send tasks in writing after meetings, even a short message? And could I sit near the window corner, away from the printer?"
Wasim thought. "Writing is easy. Honestly, the whole team would benefit. The corner, let me ask facilities."
"Thanks. I was nervous about asking. I didn't want it to sound like an excuse."
"It doesn't. It sounds like you know how you work best."
By Friday, Saurabh had the corner desk, and Wasim's messages had started arriving after every meeting.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh ask to sit?
qa.a: Near the window corner, away from the printer.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel before asking?
qa.a: Saurabh felt nervous, worried the request would sound like an excuse.

qa.q: What made Saurabh's request reasonable and easy to grant?
qa.a: Saurabh explained how the condition affects work and asked for two specific, simple changes.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the request after thinking it over?
qa.a: Wasim sees it as useful and fair, noting the whole team would benefit from written tasks.

grounding: Illustrates a young employee stating personal needs and asking a manager for reasonable workplace adjustments.

passage: For most of first year I, Jatin, hid it. I had an ADHD diagnosis from school, a letter in a drawer at home, and I told myself college would be different. It wasn't. In three-hour exams in a hall of two hundred people, I'd read question five, drift to the clock, the fan, a cough, and look up with forty minutes gone. My marks didn't match what I knew. In second year my friend Ankita, who uses a screen reader, asked why I never went to the disability cell. "They're there for this," she said. "It's not a favour." My stomach twisted the whole walk there. But I took the letter and asked, plainly, for a separate room and extra time. It took two weeks of forms. Last semester I finished every paper. I still feel a bit exposed about it, just less than I used to.

qa.q: What did Jatin ask the disability cell for?
qa.a: A separate room and extra time.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel walking to the disability cell?
qa.a: Jatin felt anxious, with a stomach that twisted the whole walk, and still feels a little exposed about asking.

qa.q: What made Jatin's request likely to succeed?
qa.a: Bringing the letter and asking plainly for specific adjustments, then following through two weeks of forms.

qa.q: How does Ankita see asking for support?
qa.a: Ankita treats support as a right rather than a favour, and says so plainly to encourage Jatin.

grounding: Shows a young adult stating a need to the college and asking for reasonable exam adjustments.
